She ' said I was working in that sad place in then, where the looms am, and all tot a sudden I Imanl above the noise of the :not:Murry a fearful and aWflll rumbling noise. I could not conceive what had happened, before Iliad time to noh to the door. I was ommol in on every side, and I cried to Duncan Brown, who was rush- ing past, to save me. I now saw that the greater part of the roof of the weft shed had fallen in, and I rement- lber seeing a big pie, of wal ellitle thump Oown on. the • tenter's • desk. Wool I was extricatol, it began to dawn on me that something terrible had happened, and I the first words I cried were, • Oh, my sister, my sister. she must be fearfully crushed. My mother is in the gatehouse, and I know she will go mad when she hears that oneof her own has been killed. I was well ac- quainted with the lassie Jeanie Clam, who is lying stretched out dead there. She waso niee bit girl. Then them is Mary Ann Stewart and Jessie Oilison ; they are also dead. I was talking to them just a little before the awful affair. All my conipanions are lying amongst the ruins, and find only, knows why I was not also among , them. Pierre de Salerne, its the department of the Fare, in France, was found inurderssl j in her own house. Some time afterwards, Louis Delano, a child of fourteen, related that, while passing Madlle. Moistens house on the evening when the murder was committesi she saw an old man, attired in a long blouse, with a white beard, bent aim, st double with age. awl j leaning 0,50 stick. Oddly enough. this was an exact description of Inc grand-uncle, Jean Delanoe, but the j girl had never been acquainted with bins, and slid not j even know his name. The judicial authorities, however. I were reluctant to sorest this patriarch of eighty-two, and J Jean Delano,. in all likelihoesl would have carried Isis fatal secret wills him to the tomb had he not been oc imprudent as to give the timepieve of the murdered woman to a local watchmaker to clean. Jean Delano was arrested, and a onfessing his galls. averred that he had killed the old lady because she accused him of running after the girls, lie has been smteneed to im- prisonment for life.
DEATH OF THE REV. G. E. YOUNG, LATE OF WARRINGTON.

The death is announced of the Rev. G. F.. Young,: who, until quite recently, was the superintendent mmisterof the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit. Dur- ing his three years' residence in Warrington, Mr. Young won the esteem and respect not only of those of his own denomination, but of the towns- people generally, and the intimation of his death will be received with widespread regret. Mr. Young entered the Weldeyan ministry early in life, and lia.l held appointments in many circuits, the last of which, before conning to II arrington, was ShetHeld. He left Warrington to commence his duties in his new circuit, the head of which was Batley, in York- shire, on the tirst of September, so that he had only been there a few weeks when 'news of his demise, winch occurred on Sunday evening, reached War- rington. He leaves a large family, one of whom is I a student for the Wesleyan ministry at Ileadingly College. Mr. Young wos a victim to a toil taken , whilst attending One of trio flock, and eventually succumbed to an attack of congestion of the kink . . . . . .

On the occaston of Ws last or 0, which he preached in Hold-st.thapel toocrowded congregation, Mr. Y. I after delivering a bmehing awl interesting ilkeourse.! ! said he could not tell them how deeply he felt his ! I enforced separation from his Warrington friew s ! had never met with kinder friends, nor more true or loving hearers. it' thanked them for theconfidenor they had always put in him. They had worked well together— : their officers, their leaders, their local preachers. their trustees and stewards and all tie members of the church ! had worked admirahty together, and with unanimity. Meowed much of hk peace awl happiness to them. Ile should never level them, and in his Yorkshire cinsia Ihe should often think oiliest, lie wished also to thank ' the choir. Many Of the services had been made all the more effective by their skilfulnitss. Mr. Young also bore testi. no to the worth ef the newly-appointed superintendent of the cireuit. the Rev. John Gunnell, and in conclusion, biped that the Methodistical year which was about to commence would be crowned with blessing and saccess.

On Saturday evening another meeting of resi- dents in Latchford was held, at Late Word railway station, to consider matters in connect ion with the proposed alteratiotm of road by the Ship Canal Co. There was a full attendance, and Mr. J. C. Parr was elected to preside. Mr. J. White. who produces! several plans, explained the position of affairs. Ile mentioned that the Canal Company were at present obliged by Act of Parliament to construct three swing bridges over the canal one at linutsford- road, one at elrappenliall-road, and one at Acker's- lane. The Company now propossal to put only one bridge over the canal in place of the two at Knutsford-road and Si rappenhall-road. It had been suggestml, he said, that the only object of the Canal Company was to save expense. but it was alleged on the sort of tile Company that they could not have these two bridges so close together as the two bridges would ben they said it would be quite impossible to work the canal with safety if they hat those two bridges so close together. Whether it wao a natural imposeibility or not he could not say, but they must take the Company's word for it. lie did not think the Company would have gone to the expense of making the new roads that hail already been made if they had foreseen this dill!- ! culty in the first instance. Be thought it wm now ' advisable for the residents of Latchford to make some arrangements with the Ship Canal Company through the Highway Board. He could not tell what the Railway Company had to my upon that question, probably they might oppose the Canal Company's bill in Parliament for more reason than ' one. • Intelligence has been received in Melbourne stating that the natives in the Solomon Islands some time ago decoyed and niordered an Englishman named Nelson and Rms native boys and devoured them. 11. M. cruiser Royalist reports that she shelled the villages on that part of the coast where the massacre occurred, and that the natives ttssl to the fields. div.head: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN AMERICA.
div.p: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN AMERICA.

A farmer named Westbrook, living at Vergenets. Miehigan, became insane owing to his financial troubles and destroys,' the lives of his family in a horrible manner. Ile attacked his wife with a haminer, bi•at her skull and killed her. /le then treated each of Ms three daughters in the saine way, and finally attempted to kill his son. The latter, however. simeeeded in diAtnning IVesthrook, who fled, awl committed suicide by cutting his throat with a rasor.

div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.

In London, an Wednesday, a ease came before Mr. Justice Denman in which a young woman of 23, named Laws, sought to recover damages for breach of pro- mise, from Mr. C. L. Capron, a soltor over 80 years of , age. The plaintiff alleged that after the death of Ids wife, the defendant took apartments in the boom in ' which she lived, and than made her acquaintance. Ile had offered her marriage, and had admitted his liability by offering her £l,OOO in settlement of her claim. She proposed to read a solicitor's letter in which theoffer was ' made, but the defendant's counwl said the solicitor to 1 whom the plaintiff referred had never acted for the defendant, and had, in fact, at one time been the plain- ' tiff's solicitor, and the letter was not admitted. The ! plaintiff had no witnesses except herself, and the learned Judge, explaining that corroboration of her story was essentixl, nonsuited her.

div.head: SAMPSON AND MS RIVALS.
div.p: SAMPSON AND MS RIVALS.

The competition between" Samson," " the strongest man on earth," and Sundown, the young Russian athlete, took place at the Royal Aquarium, Westminister on Saturday night. The hall was quite crowded by a greatly excited audience. Captain AlolwAvorth, the chairman of the Aquarium Company, announced, upon Samson's appearance, that the Marquis of Queensberry, and Lord de Clifford, would net as judges ; and or Sam- , lon now nyjuired that there should Ins stake on both sides, the Royal Aquarium directors undertook to place £lOO against his stake. Sandows having in turn per- , formed Samson's tests of bending an iron rod across his I arm, breaking a piece of wire hy expansion of the chest, and breaking iron rings on his arms, the champion ' ' challenged irk rival to do certain feats, but did not lead ' off. Tiro judges then decided time Sandows should rho , some feats of his own, and the young athlete caught I hold of one of the gentlemen on the stage, and lifted I him at arm's length, arid lifted several weighty, one scaling 1501b0., over his head. Samson having declined to proceed, Captain Afolesworth announced that the judges had decided in favour of Sandows.

The Corporation of Warrington are to be con- gratulated on coming If victorious in what is known an the Winwick-road obstmetion case. The issue has been fairly fought (int ; and it is a matter , of course now to presume that the appellant was in the wrong. As the Bench were less than live minutes in conning to Is decision, it is obvious that, , in their judgment, the ease for the Corporation 11 was impregnable.

Mr John Morley has been anderthe tire, at New- castle, of the Labour Electoral Association : and ,he has stood it very well. He does not subscribe !to all the points of their far-reaching charter; I but he lets it be seen that he is to be classed an a Racheal Reformer. He is in favour of manhood 18nd:rage, one man—one vote, payment of Inmabers, Free Education, :nal reforms of the HOW. of Lords. Good, very good ; it is something to be going on with.

As it is only right to give a lift on the way, it should he mentioned that St. James's Church, Latchford, seems to stand in need of another of Sir Gilbert's amines. There has been a sale ed work this week, " The offertories not having been sufficiently large to pay expenses." It would 8001 s that St. James's is like most of sac—it is in a state of chronic impecunhosity. Why, oh, why, cannot we all be helped by a sale of work "every year ?" -N.B.—the "P.D." says helms a sale id his work " every week:" he therefore claims to be recognized as a very high Churchman.,

A Tory contemporary ridiculously alleges that !Councillor IV Pierpoint, at thu dinner to thu Mayor, said, referring to Alderman Crostield : I" He always talked alt of nonsense whenever he got Up to speak." There were no reporters pre- sent ; hut we are indhorised to deny that he used any such language. These who are familiar with Conneiflor nerpoint know that he does not speak of his foes in such a style —to say notl g of his Molds. It may Ito that the inventor if the phrase pit in inverted commas prides himself upon again hoaxing his readers ; but the joke, if it he a joke, is as very poor one.

Smoking is on the increase ; but are we the better for it That ia a question which is beginni ll gto be iliseussed. On Monday eve ll ill g, in Wycliffe School, Warrington, there will be a lecture on the subject by Dr. Martin of Manchester, and formerly Warrington. The chair is to be taken at a quarter to eight.

A BRISTOL WOMAN ALLEGES THAT SHE FELL

_ AMoNii THIEVES. Harriet Carter. a decently attired woman, who gave her age a'2o years, win, charged at the Warrington Police Court. on Monday. with drunkenness. It was stated that she came to the Bri.lewell on Saturday night, in a state of drunkenness, and desired to be locked up. She was at that time " wearing " a very bad black eye, and the police officials acceded to her n.quest. When she was awaiting trial on Monday she care- fully held her handkerchief to her face, but when ehe took her place in the dock the magistrates anked that she would remove it. She did no, and disclosed to view the optic in question, which was so badly injured as to cause something liken senation in the Court. She admitted having had too much drink, but declared that three men, taking advantage of her condition, had snatched her purse from her I band. as well as stolen her hat. When she cried out, one of the men struck her and gave her a black eye. She had, she said, come from Bristol to look for her husband, who was working on the Canal. She had intended to go back to Bristol, but all her money, 12s. lit., was in the purse that was stolen, and now she had nothing. The magistrates directed that eht ehould be discharged. AN EABLEBTOWN Boy CHARGED WITH OBTAINING MONEY BY FALfin PRETENCES. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, ahoy named William Taylor, (1:31, who lives at Earlestown, was brought up on remand on a charge of having on two occasions, obtained money by false pretences from the Rev. H. Monk, vicar of Newton. Mr. Monks said that on the 18th of last month prisoner called at his house, and on the plea that his little brother was dangerously ill and in need of nourishment, obtained a florin from him. On the 20th October witnena gave the lad 2e. Csi., believing his story to he true. On the following day, the reverend gentleman went to the house of the prisoner's mother, in Derby-st.. Earles- town, and then ascertained that the lad's tale was a fabrication. Sergeant Longworth informed the Bench that he had been prosecuting inquiries regarding the prison. r, and had discovered that there were twelve charges that might have been preferred against him. The magistrates ordered that the lad should be sent loan Industrial School until he reaches the age of sixteen years. The Rev. 11. Monk, when the case was over, said that he had prosecuted with the hope that that course would be taken.

TILE DEATH AN-il NEGLECT OF POOR THOMAS
SILtW.

Sir,—The inquest on the death of poor rhoutaA Shaw, who met with a fatal accident on the Ship Canal near Thelwall, on Thursday, October 31st, was held on Satur- day last, at the hospital. Mr. 11•VidS011 was elected foreman of the jury, and a verdict of accidental death was returned. The jury, through their foreman, called the attention of the Coroner to the state of the corpse. It had not been laid out, nor had the face been washed. The Coroner said, if desired to do to, he would bring the matter heron. Mr. Walker, the contractor ; he was sur- prised at the net-glees. Mr. Ewart, the under agent wino represented Mr. Walker M the ateenye of the agent (win. was in London) asked that the agent should be written to instead of Mr. Walker, and the mattor uonald undoubtedly be attended to. Ibis the Coroner said he would see that awe. On Monday the pow man was buried at Oughtrington, and Irene unimpeachable authority I am informed that but for Mrs. Scully. who livm inn cottage near the hos- pital, the matt weadd have been buried as Inc was taken from las work. Mrs. Scully washed his fare, and the undertakers. tok off hisbOOLS: the corpse was then placed in the coffin and taken to the grave without any further attention. AA a jUrOT, who has heard much of Mr. Walker's ennuderation for his employes, 1 must protest against such indecency. I do no more espwially no there have 1..... a cases previously where due attention has not bean paid tithe corpse at this place. Who is to shame? Ido not know; knit I hope there will be no repetition of such flagrant carelessness and indifference as was too apparent in the case of poor Shaw.—Yours, A JUROR.

Nothing, he said. gave hint greater pleaSllle. and particularly on °ermines of that kind, than to .50- I ciate with the men with whom he was daily brought in- to contact. He was very thankful ti find himself , lamongst such a staff. As men esineerned with public , lamas there were many strangers in their midst, as they were constantly being 1,111, Med from One section to ; another, but he could safely say that there was no clam of people more affectionate to each other. The day previously be had ; completed his second year on the Acton Grange section.
